For example a majority of people would not use the term Latinx or AAPI, and they’re a majority who would use BIPOC as well. I wonder what their personal reason is for not using these words. I believe that it is because the people themselves that are apart of these groups don’t like the use of these words to describe them, for example, I don’t know any Latino person who wants to be called Latinx. raw_comment: My first reaction to this graph was surprise. I think that it is so interesting to see all the different names for one ethnic group that I’ve never heard of before or would never even think to call someone. Through observing this graph, I noticed how the words that were commonly used, were the phrases that I’ve heard spoken the most around me. I was also surprised to see that the acronym phrases, A.A Pi and BIPOC were used a fair bit, being phrases that I have never even heard of before. It's interesting to think about how different words impact other cultures and how it's essential to recognize how certain words are seen as respectful, while others may be derogatory. Talking to others, you should always be mindful of the racial terms you are using to address them, because you don't not know how a certain phrase will affect them. Regarding this,  it is important to acknowledge the cultures of others in my community because we are a very diverse town, filled with many different races of people. Recognizing how certain phrases and words impact those around us, is necessary for a connected and prosperous world.

raw_comment:
1) I noticed that some of the traditional terms that are used are being answered with "yes" rather than "no." From this, it's not absurd to assume that majority of people are content without the use of some of these newer terms like "Latinx." Of course, this doesn't mean we should just allow that smaller percentage to be uncomfortable. 
2) I wonder which generations were answering in this survey. As time passed, terms became more acceptable or more understandably offensive. Many older people still use some of these terms, though. When they were younger, those were normal things to say and call people every day and nobody would be bothered. 
3) This relates to me because I'm of very mixed heritages, so I have immersed myself with so many people from different places in my life. My maternal grandmother is native South Korean and she tells me stories from when she was younger and her experiences in Korea. So much has changed since then, including language. 
I would call this graph "What are the proper terms to refer to people with?"

raw_comment:
After looking at this graph, I noticed that many people prefer to use terms that are not older. Terms like BIPOC or AAPI are less popular than terms like Asian or Person of Color which have been around for decades. These people have probably been using these terms for years, and they may be unaware of the new terms and what has become disrespectful. 
This article led me to wonder what people of that descent would prefer to be called. I would like to ask an African American, or Black, person which term they would prefer. I don’t know who was interviewed in this article, so it might be just a bunch of white people. Of course, as a white person, I do not have any say in what terms should or should not be used, but I would like to speak to someone who does to figure out which terms are perceived as offensive and which are inclusive.
I live in the South, which is known for being highly conservative and not very progressive, so I still hear terms that are highly offensive and have been widely avoided. Although many people still use words that are offensive where I live, plenty of people are trying to change the terms they use.
I would name this graph “Offensive or Inclusive?”

raw_comment:
According to the article, the terms “Latinx”, “AAPI”, “BIPOC”, and “Nonwhite” are the 4 least popular terms in the article.
The term Latinx is often criticized as it does not read like a Spanish word whatsoever. ‘Latinx’ as a term was never intended to be used in Spanish, however I still agree with many Latinos that a word derived from Latin-America should be feasibly pronounced in Spanish. Though ‘Latino’ is a masculine adjective, masculine terms in Spanish are often used as a neutral term as well. If a more neutral term is still desired, you can use Latin-American. I’ve also heard ‘e’ be suggested as a gender-neutral suffix in Spanish, which at least makes sense to say out loud. I described myself as Latine for a time while figuring out my gender, and I enjoyed useing the term-- however I can’t really speak for others as I have lived a much whiter life than a Latino one.
The low usage of AAPI is likely caused by a mix of it not being as widely known to most people as other terms, and the fact that it conflates two different ethnic groups.
The term BIPOC has been used to replace the term POC by some, but it is a new term and from what I can tell it has very little difference from POC. Very few people feel the need to change to the new term due to what is often read as redundancy.
I have no comments on the term nonwhite.

Note that I am not a person of color! If I've said anything ignorant or hurtful, please let me know. No explanation needed, unless you want to give one.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that within this graph it shows the different use of words that Americans or a well-meaning person can say to describe the different races. The highest percentage of americans that use the terms that voted yes was for the term Hispanic with a percentage of 87%. However the term that had the lowest percentage of the people that voted yes for the use of the term to describe the different race was Latinx with a percentage of 22%. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what some of the unfamiliar terms such as BIPOC or A.A.P.I stand for. On the other hand I also wondered if people still feel offended even if they were described as "person of color" or "nonwhite" or even "BIPOC" regardless of the context or even if it's being said by a well-meaning person or not. I wonder if that makes a difference. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because we are a community of minorities and a very high percentage of the population within my community are hispanic or latinos. However we haven't really come across any americans that have described our race as "Latinx", the most common terms for us to be called would be hispanic or latino/a. It's interesting to hear the many different terms that are used that wouldn't be common for me or others in this community. 

What's going on in this graph?
"The Diversity In Terms: What Would You Say?"

raw_comment:
The percentages that stood out to me the most were "person of color" and "nonwhite". I noticed that even though the percentage wasn't over 50% it was still pretty high. I don't agree with using those terms for one it doesn't even make sense, 2 people can be the same color but completely different ethnicities. Saying nonwhite just makes it seem like any other race besides white is inferior and is all classified as one. 
I think most of the terms that were used for the chart are pretty common and I think adding more terms and asking more people would help get a more accurate representation on what terms people actually use. Or maybe not even listing terms at all and just asking without giving options would get more of an honest opinion. 
I have never heard anyone use the terms BIPOC, A.A.P.I., or Latinx before so the fact that the percentages were all over 20% with the amount of people that were asked surprised me. I wonder where the people that use those terms grew up and how they were taught about those three terms. 
The people in my community from what I hear use the most common terms the like African American, black, and Asian although I do hear a lot of people use the term Mexican instead of Hispanic which I don't agree with because if you are Mexican that means you're from Mexico and you can still be Hispanic just from different countries so I think Hispanic would be more appropriate for the overall use.

People should learn to call others by their correct name, or their name in general.

raw_comment:
After looking at this graph, and reading the article, I wasn’t too surprised by the results. There is so many different terms used these days to describe people, because no one wants to offend anyone. It’s hard to please everyone with the terms we use, and different people prefer to be called different things. Instead of using one word we think would be best, I think we should ask specific people with what they are comfortable with. For example, lots of people like to be called African American, and that's what I’m used to saying as well. But, sometimes, it’s not the correct term to use. For example, you can be Brazilian or Jamaican, so that term wouldn’t fit. That’s why I think it’s important to ask others instead of basing what we say off of one graph. 
          Some of the terms on this graph I have never even heard before, and if lot’s of people say they say it, I wonder if that's accurate. Are people putting certain responses based off what they think sounds the best?
           In my community, I hear many terms that I would never dare saying. I live in the South, and go to high school, and I hear people say things in the hallways that they would never say to their grandparents. If my school took a survey, offensive terms would have extremely high percentages, which is so very sad. I think it’s best

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I noticed that more encompassing terms are used less than specific ones. Terms like hispanic, asian, or african american were largely used more than latinx, bipoc, or aapi. Furthermore, stating someone's specific background outweighed the use of all the more general phrases such as "people of color" or "non-white," that category having every term be not used by over 50% of Americans. Out of all the terms, Americans would say Hispanic the most (87%) and Latinx the least (22%). 
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder what was the racial demographic of the Americans surveyed, as well as their age range. From my point of view, the terms that seem to be used less in the graph are used more by younger, marginalized people, rather than those who are older and aren't used to certain descriptors.  
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because amongst my generation there has been a push for more inclusive language, which as seen by the graph consists of the terms being used the least.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
This graph shows different words, and the percent of Americans that would or would not say them. My headline would be "Identifiers, Which ones are Americans Using?"

raw_comment:
When I was looking at the graph I saw that almost all the phrases that were lower than 50% in the yes column, were words that I have never heard said in person. I think that an important thing to clarify in the question is, is it in front of the person, or just even in person. People are much bolder behind people’s backs, and on the internet, so I think that this clarification should be made. I also noticed how there was only one word in the middle of the graph, and that was the phrase, person of color. All the others were either a strong yes or a strong no. I don’t know why this one is as contradicting as the other ones. All I know is that this phrase is very vague since a person of color could be anyone since we are all just different colors.

After looking at the graph, I asked myself if I would use them, and I realized that I would only use 4 out of the 11 words listed. raw_comment: This graph surprised me in many ways. First of all I have never heard the terms Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC. I’m also surprised Americans said those terms at all because I don’t even know what they mean. I feel like a lot of Americans are hesitant to use many racial terms these days because a lot of words and names can be interpreted and taken as racist. I think it's harder for older people to respect people of other races because when they were younger, many of those terms were normal and what everyone used so that's just what they are used to calling people with different races than them. I feel also that gen-z does a great job respecting what people want to be called when referring to their race. I once saw a YouTube survey video where people were asked what they were comfortable with people calling their race and the results were all very different so I believe the best way to figure out what you should call people with a different race is just ask them what they are comfortable with. I'm sure anyone would love to hear that you are curious and care about respecting what they want to be referred to as.

raw_comment:
What I first noticed about this graph is that the first word of each graph is what I would assume is the most baseline way to refer to someone of color. I myself am Hispanic and I have only overheard the word "Latinx" less than three times in my life. I don't know exactly what it means, if it is different from Hispanic or Latino. Whenever I have been referred to as Latinx I haven't felt insulted or disrespected. 
This relates to my community because there are several things that my Hispanic family and friends would feel insulted if someone used specific words to allude our Mexican heritage. I always thought and still do think that Hispanic is the most respectful way to refer to someone of Mexican heritage. I cannot speak my opinion for any other of these graphs because I am Hispanic so I don't know how any other person about their heritage personally feels.
But, I have always mentioned people from Asia or have heritage from Asia as Asians. And people of darker skin color as African American. Because that is what I always believed was to be the most respectful way to say it.
This graph is just showing what the majority of American Adults refer to people of different heritage. I have always believed that there is no need to call anyone by these names unless it is asked. I would never bluntly call someone by one of these names, I would always just call them by their name. I just don't feel that it is needed because we are all just human beings.

raw_comment: Looking at the graph I see the different terms people have started using to describe other people, I have at least heard all of these terms once, I've seen some others used more online than in person and some “main '' others that are used in real life in the south where I live. It's not surprising to me that some terms are used more than others, each label has a different name but relatively in each category all mean the same, some more inclusive than others. I wonder if some of the terms people use are because they believe it makes them “woke” and what other people use only because it's the only term they know and were taught and grew up with. I would also like to see a graph of what the ages are and the age gaps between what the older generation uses and the younger generation uses, what they think of each term and how they feel about it. I don’t think I can have a say in this as a cisgender white person in the south, this isn’t my community or my ground to say what terms are “better than others” each term has its own history and can be important to some people and unimportant to others it all comes down to perspective. I think the article name “Terms of the U.S and what they mean to you”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice that the most commonly used terms that are used to describe race/ethnicity are mainly the ones that are used in the media ex., broadcasts, newspapers, and social media. I feel like people are hesitant to use words that they feel do not seem correct or that will offend someone.

What do you wonder?

I wonder why the term "African American" is used more than the term "Black". This just surprised me for some reason.

How does this relate to you and your community?

I feel like this relates to me and my community because people I hear the words people say when they refer to races. I think the words people used to describe a race reflect where they grow up and whom they are surrounded by.

What's going on in this graph?

This graph demonstrates the words people use to describe specific races/ethnicities and why. People differentiate these words from appropriate to say and what is offensive to say.

Catchy Headline:

Think Before You Speak

raw_comment:
To me, this graph speaks volumes on what society is and how we have decided to combat racism. I replied to another New York Times article on an issue of racism and how a mural in a Law School is under the decision of removal after many onlookers felt uncomfortable with its art style and its portrayal of slavery. My opinion was that the ones who should decide what should happen with the mural should be the same people who were affected by what the mural depicts. Personally, being Caucasian, I don’t experience racism as someone of color or race would and I'm not as affected by it but I can try to give my voice of reason.
  In this day and age people forget what can be offensive and try to stick on the side that likely has no negative connotations. Calling someone “black” or “asian” to some 20% of people is not a term they would use but to the majority, these terms aren’t racist and rather are just a descriptive feature that is provided when they look at someone. Similar to what I said in my comment on the mural, I believe that the people who decide whether a term is offensive or not should be decided by the group that is going to be called or referred to by those terms.

raw_comment: When I first read the graph, I wasn't too shocked by the information. Most words I’d recognized and the ones with higher percentages were more familiar to me because I feel like I see those most in the media. I've rarely heard people use the term “Latinx” and I feel it's pretty much the same as “Latino/a”. But I've never even seen the terms “A.A.P.I” or “BIPOC”, so it surprises me that those have any “yes” percentage at all, and I wonder if people truly use those terms or if they were just trying to seem inclusive on the survey. My town is predominantly white, according to the census, white Americans make up 74.4% of our community. Black or African American people make up 17.2% and all the other races combined make up the last 8.4%. So, I think it's important to refer to people in a respectful way, but I think all of the terms included on the graph would be perfectly civil to call someone, it only gets rude when people use other terms. The name of this graph though, could be improved. I would probably title it “racial titles in 2023” because that gives the reader more of an idea of what the graph will be about, but it's still concise.

raw_comment:
This chart has terms such as “Latinx” and “BIPOC” which I've heard rarely and don’t necessarily know what they stand for. And after researching them they seem to be very inclusive but fairly new. Not many people in my area refer to others using “Latinx”, “BIPOC”, or “A.A.I.P” and usually stick to the more vague terms such as  “Asian” or “Hispanic”. I can see why they aren’t very popular in this study of about 4,500 people with “no” percentages of 78% for Latinx and 70% for BIPOC, likely because as I stated above, they are generally newer terms coming out in the 2000s. It makes sense that newer terms, especially related to race and ethnicity, are not used in order to avoid offending others because the meaning has not yet been globalized. While everyone can do a quick google search, just as I did, many people don’t care to look or even know to look, thus resulting in a large population that doesn’t understand the terms used above. This is why some of the most popular terms are “Hispanic” or “Asian” when asked if Americans use certain terms when referring to race and ethnicity. Even though they are pretty vague, most people don’t know any better. It’s obvious that the longer a word is around for, the more widely accepted it's going to be in contrast to newer terms.

raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
It looks like terms relating to “Black”and “African American” received overwhelming positive feedback as words Americans would say compared to any other category. More specifically, “Black” received a “yes” vote of 75% and a “no” of 25% & “African American” received 77% “yes” and 23% “no”.

What do you wonder?
I wonder why a overwhelming majority of people said “no” to using the term “Latinx”. More specifically, 78% of respondents said “no.” 

How does this relate to you and your community? 
This relates to me and my community because I have friends who are Hispanic and Asian and it is interring to see what terms are more commonly used that others when referring to people groups and ethnicities. 

Alternate headline: 
“11 words & 4,423 responses; this is how we talk about each other in 2023.”

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed from the graph that the Americans who responded to this survey decided to say more simple words instead of complex identity words. For example, 81% of Americans are okay with referring to people as Asians, but when it comes to more inclusive terms like A. A. P. I, only 27% say yes to using the term. The same thing goes for the 75% of Americans who say black people compared to 30% who don't say B.I.P.O.C. I noticed this in the graph for the term Latinx, which is more inclusive towards people, yet Americans prefer saying Latino/Latina.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how the results of the graph would differ if a different group of people were interviewed. Do these types of results only vary so much because it's Americans or do all groups of people think this way? Do the results look like this because we're still waiting for these terms to gain popularity? Or is it a thing of racism?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and me because I fall under the Hispanic, Latino/Latina, and Latinx categories, and it is very interesting to see what people prefer to call groups with ethnic backgrounds. This also informs me of what Americans refer to me and my community as. 


What's going on in this graph?
"Say YES to the word! What terms are appropriate in this new era?"

raw_comment:
This graph is showing the result of what 4,423 Americans refer to people of different races or ethnicities as. I first noticed Americans are very comfortable using the terms “Hispanic and Asian”. Yet Americans rarely use the terms “BIPOC or A.A.P.I”. I wonder why people are more comfortable saying Hispanic or Asian, maybe because they wanted to be “with the crowd”. I’m not sure if there’s a specific reason why people don’t use the specific terms but they’ll use the overall “popular” ethnicity names. I mean this could be to avoid awkward conversations or situations by calling someone the wrong ethnicity, but I do think you could just ask what they would prefer to be called in general. 
  I also wonder in this survey what the ratio of people of different ethnicities to white was. I think this survey could be biased or unreliable information if the ratio wasn’t close to equal. I think they should have done a counter survey to see which terms people of different ethnicities would prefer to be called. With that kind of information we could see the differences and make comments about how they differ and which terms are more comfortable for a person of different ethnicity. I do think using general terms to someone of different ethnicity could be disrespectful in some situations, because if someone is not the ethnicity you assumed, you just called them something they weren’t and that's disrespectful. That's why I always ask what someone would prefer to be called before I assume.

raw_comment:
These days you can offend just about anyone when it comes to talking about race. I think when there is tension in a room because of the topic it’s because some believe they are very advanced and educated in this area compared to others. They take advantage of the opportunity to express their view to you in a way that can degrade one's confidence. I don’t understand why people have to get all offended and flip out when I genuinely don’t understand the difference between Hispanic and Latino. I mean shouldn’t you be proud of your heritage and excited to teach someone something new. I think in these heated conversations we should start using them as a teaching moment rather than making one feel less of themselves for not knowing something they weren’t taught. 
   Seeing that more people use the word Hispanic than Latinx is because of the fear of being perceived as insensitive. I can understand one not saying Latinx because they don’t fully know what it means and are fearful of being hammered for being incorrect. Personally I think it’s sad that folks are just afraid to be politically incorrect choosing the phrase people of color rather than nonwhite. I mean can’t we just offer each other grace. Not everyone has grown up in a household where they talk about diversity, its beauty and what is/isn’t offensive.

raw_comment:
In this graph, I see that our society has become hyper focused on labeling each other and fitting into specific groups. Although this graph is about race, an age-old concept, many of the terms didn’t exist until now and are just starting to be used more often. As the world has become more culturally and racially inclusive, we have also realized that maybe some of these phrases are too wide-ranging. Although the newer terms, such as “Latinx” and “BIPOC” haven’t gained a ton of popularity yet, they are starting to catch on. I think this is a good thing for the world because it emphasizes smaller groups within larger ethnic groups. Some of these people may have previously been underrepresented and giving them a specific name can help give them the recognition that they deserve. I also think that sometimes people will use the broader terms, like “Asian” or “Hispanic” at times when it may be more appropriate to use a more particular term. I have noticed at school or around town, people who use these broader terms tend to generalize a group of people, sometimes even stereotype them.

raw_comment: The graph claims to have data for what people call ethnic groups by asking if you would or would not call a certain ethnic group a particular name. But how do you know that the graph is presenting accurate data? When you collect data you represent the average of the data you collected but there’s also so many people that weren’t represented of the terms people would use. Also what if the graph is asking a question that people can’t answer one way or the other entirely and are forced to just choose one? Does this affect the data? I feel like this graph is very relatable though because you can look at the top one in each ethnic group and know what you should openly call these ethnic groups as well as words you should be more careful with to make sure they are not taken offensively, and overall educates you on the terminology you should use. raw_comment: The first thing I notice when I look at this graph is how many people don’t like the term “Latinx”. I’d never heard of it before and it made me wonder why people seem to dislike it so much. I understand the context behind why it was made, to be a gender neutral alternative to Latino/Latina, and I guess since nonbinary people are a minority it would make sense why most people prefer not to use it. It reminded me of the term “Womxn” which was made as a gender neutral alternative to the word “Woman” but isn’t nearly as inclusive as people act like it is. Although it claims to be more inclusive of trans women, the label just treats them like they’re not real women by making a specific term to separate them from other women. This reminded me of how, in my community (LGBTQ+), there’s often a lot of controversy about what labels or pride flags are outdated and appropriate to use. For example, the progress pride flag was made to highlight trans and POC queer people, but some people don’t like that they’re highlighted in that design because it makes it seem like they weren’t included in the original rainbow flag. The trend I notice on this graph is that most people prefer more general terms like “Asian” rather than “A.A.P.I.” probably because the newer terms that are made to be more inclusive tend to make the people they’re trying to include only feel more isolated. I would probably title this graph “Preferred Racial Terminology of 2023”.

raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I noticed that the graph represents quite a few words that Americans won't repeat and this is shown using different colors to represent yes and no answers. most people won't say words that they aren't familiar with. This is apparent with the Latinx, AAPI, and the BIPOC. Of all the terms on this graph, LATINX is used the least with only 22% of people confirming they say it.

I wonder how this graph came to be and what group was studied. I also wonder why people aren't comfortable with using terms such as AAPI or BIPOC. Could it be because they don't know what it stands for?

3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because it is made up of mostly hispanics/latinos. Most hispanics aren't on the internet often, so they may be more comfortable using shorter terms than longer ones they aren't used to.

raw_comment:
1.) What do I wonder?
- I wonder what age groups were polled for this sample, and if that affects the overall percentages. I am also curious to know if those who voted no (for any of the terms) simply just are not used to the word, or if they would not feel comfortable saying it etc.

2.) What do I notice?
- I notice that for the terms Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC those who voted “no” surpass those who voted “yes” by a very large percent. While there are multiple terms for each category, there is one specific term that most people tend to be comfortable saying. I think the terms with high percentages are the ones most often used, and many people most likely follow the language others use. 

3.) Catchy Headline: “Societies correct and incorrect terminologies”

raw_comment:
1. The incorporation of these new terms to refer to ethnic groups that are inclusive like Latinx that doesn't strictly bind the person to gender is a good turn for the time as Gender is not only male and female and I would predict that percentage will grow in a few years to help with respect when referring to specific people. It's extremely amusing that many individuals might not even understand what terms like AAPI, LatinX, or BiPoc imply. It took me looking them up to realize when these terms demand respect when referring to a person.
2. I'm curious as to why Latino/Latina is used less frequently than Hispanic, despite the fact that the only distinction between the two terms is how the male and feminine pronouns are assigned to the word. Also, I've never heard of the terms A.A.P.I. or BIPOC, but after some research, I learned that they stand for "Asian American/Pacific Islander" and "Black Indigenous Person of Color". I'm curious whether the Americans who claimed they didn't use those terms did so because they, like me, had never heard of them or for some other purpose.
3. This relates to my community and me because being a Peruvian woman as well as my family being from South America, we are considered Latino and Hispanic. I also live in a place where many people from Latin America self-identify as Hispanic or Latino, which is intriguing to contrast with the chart since I have never heard any of my friends identify as Latinx.
4. Which Do YOU Identify? Check All That Apply.

raw_comment:
I notice that people are generally more inclined to use terms that have been around for longer for these groups of people. This is shown by how for each newer terms such as Latinx and A.A.P.I. there is a large majority that said they would not use these terms but would be more likely to make use of terms such as Hispanic and Asian which is supported by the large majority saying they would use these terms. 

           I feel as though that these new terms are so obsolete to the vast majority to the population that they are not really the "politically correct"  terms or at least should not be. Most people that I know that are Asian, Black, Hispanic, etc. are fine with me using the just mentioned terms and they are ok with others saying these things as well. I think that the large majority of those groups should be able to decide what is correct and what is not as it pertains to them more than anyone else. If they were able to decide it seems that as long as this study was unbiased, which hopefully it was, then they would accept the more "common" terms.

             A fitting name for the graph would be "Terms for Peoples of Different Racial Backgrounds and How the American Population Uses Them".

raw_comment:
Upon observing the graph, I noticed that the sample size of Americans surveyed was relatively small, consisting of only 4,423 individuals out of the almost 332 million residing in the USA. 
It was also interesting to note that many Americans used terms such as Hispanic, African American, and Asian when referring to people of color.
 This is not surprising, given the prevalence of social media and its impact on shaping individuals' perspectives on ethnicity. 
For example, the term Latinx has been controversial among the Hispanic/Latino community, with some finding it offensive. The graph's significance lies in its reflection of the language and attitudes of Americans as a collective group. Depending on one's race, ethnicity, or gender, they may be more or less likely to use certain words. 
Moreover, the graph is relevant to individuals interested in promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion, as it sheds light on language habits and preferences of different demographic groups. 
Some questions that the graph may provoke include the factors that influence people's language choices, why certain terms are more common than others, and how language use reflects cultural and social changes over time. By analyzing the data, one can gain insights into language patterns among different communities and raise questions about the inclusiveness of language use in their own community.

raw_comment:
Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Person of Color. What these terms all have in common is that they are broad, umbrella terms used to describe people of varying ethnicities. What I inferred from this graph is that people use terms that make them feel the most comfortable to avoid offending others. However, I don’t think we should focus on what makes us comfortable, and instead use the term that the people who are of these ethnicities identify with. 
When the Black Lives Matter movement first gained momentum, I remember hearing the broad terms in the news, but I also remember seeing interviews and articles talking about “which term is the best” and “which terms are offensive”. People debating if POC was offensive or not, or which terms included which ethnicities. Beyond that, we put so much energy into arguing over these characterizations when we should be focusing on equality and respecting others regardless of their ethnicity instead.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the graphs key specifically says that the question is being asked to Americans. I also notice that the options are split up by racial/ethnic group and that the least favored option by ethnic group is the last term.

2. To build off of my notice I wonder what were the ethnic and racial groups of the Americans being asked as well as the backgrounds of those Americans. An African American and a Latino American will likely not have the same views as an Asian American person. I also wonder how diverse the survey was in terms of age not just race or ethnicity as that may change the outlook and responses generations may have on certain terms.

3. Since I'm Hispanic(of a spanish speaking country) ethnically and of African descent racially, I have differing opinions to other people who may be exclusively one or the other, personally I have no issue with the term Latino/Latina, or Black, but from what I have been told by my community, peers, and elders is that terms like "Latinx" or "African American" can be seen as offensive due to the way it clashes with culture. I was told that not all people of African Descent are American, (referring to "Afro-caribbeans") and that "Latinx" does not fit into the spanish language, as the spanish language is "built on gendered words." These are explanations I have found from a varying amount of people, and it doesn't even scratch the surface.

4. What would you say?

raw_comment:
In the chart, I notice people are more comfortable using "umbrella terms" than more specific terms and labels. Using more specific terms like Latinx and Asian American can be good but I think you should know some of the person's background before referring to their label. For example, Latino/Latina are referring to people from Latin America so it would be incorrect to refer to someone from Spain as Latino. The more correct term would be Hispanic. 
    I wonder if people were already more familiar with these terms the statistics would be different. If people correctly educated themselves on these titles then people could correctly refer to a group of people, instead of incorrectly labeling them. It would help make groups more diverse instead of generalizing. For instance, it would be incorrect to say every black person was African American because not every black person has descent from Africa. Many people have descent and traditions from Brazil, Haiti, Columbia, etc.
     Even though there is a big white population at my school, there are still many POC and my area can be very diverse. People should learn about how to refer to groups of people because it can make people feel more comfortable since POC groups seem to be smaller around me. A good way to title this graph could be "Educate your way of speech".

raw_comment:
While looking at this graph, something that catches my attention is how spread out peoples choice of words are. Though 4,423 people isn't a huge amount, it gives me a lot of perspectives of how many address race. I definitely see how careless it can be to call someone "nonwhite" or "Black", not only because you might not know their ethnicity, but because how antique those words are. I say antique because those words are truly outdated, and wouldn't be a regular thing to call someone.
          I do believe that it's very important to find out what a person is comfortable with being called, because ethnicity and race are two different things. I can see that the surveyed group who used terms like "nonwhite" might have been influenced wrongly from their parents or media. I also see that a huge percentage of the surveyed group are most comfortable with terms like "Hispanic" and "Asian", which are also common terms I hear around my community.
           Research is an important tool to use if you are in the topic of race and ethnicity. You never know how calling someone one of these terms can effect how you are viewed. This might be why some of the people surveyed used terms such as "BIPOC" and "AAPI". It could be because they might be afraid to use a wrong term, or because they prefer to use a newer and thoughtful term. Overall, this article shows me a a list of terms that people think are more valuable to be heard by an audience of people with mixed ethnicity and race.

PART 1
1. I notice that each section begins with the general term of the group and the percentages of yesses are higher and nos are lower and as the list goes down, the group term becomes more specified and the percentages are switched. 2. I wonder how the percentage would be different if people were more familiar with the specified terms. I think if people become more familiar with it, then we could correctly use them to address a group and it allows diversity rather than putting a group of people under one name.

raw_comment:
This graph is interesting to me because it depicts how humans are so afraid to be wrong; to be judged by others. While some would say LatinX, the majority wouldn’t, either because they don’t know what it means, or because they are scared they could possibly offend someone by using the term wrong, or even worse; using the wrong term.
	People should start becoming more knowledgeable about the terms associated with the different races of the world, because the simple terms like “black”, “asian” and “hispanic”, are extremely vague in regard to what someone ethnicity truly is. As a whole, humans are so scared of being wrong, or even worse, being canceled that they would not ask a question, get to know someone. 
	If you are to speak about others' race or ethnicity to others, or if someone is speaking to you about theirs, having knowledge of the terms they may use to describe themselves is important to getting to know who someone truly is. Because there is a big difference between “non white” and “BIPOC”. The world just needs to be inclusive of everyone, and that means using the right ethnic names.

raw_comment: There is always a reason behind every graph or statistic, and I think the reason for why the words like “nonwhite”, “BIPOC”, “A.A.P.I”, and “Latinx” are statistically less used is that they are less traditional terms for groups of people, and the main people who use them more than likely inhabit the hyper politically correct sector of humans. For example, according to the Journal of Hispanic Higher Education, the first instance of the term Latinx in academic literature was in 2013. This means that the word has not really had much time to catch on to the general populace. Another example would be the term A.A.P.I, which I had never heard of. This term was first introduced in the 80s, so is much newer than most of the other terms like Asian American, or Asian. I would guess that the older the term, the more popular it is, and vice versa with younger terms. The main thing I do not understand about this graph is the percentage of people that would not say anything about anyone's race. I would have to guess that they would claim to not see color and so they have nothing to say about it, but I cannot be sure. Personally, most of the people I know (including me) use the most popular term for each category and there does not seem to be much fuss among us, but there will always be a person that wants to change things up. If I had to come up with a headline for this graph, it would be something along the lines of “Majority of Americans prefer to use terms that are older, study shows.”

raw_comment:
Looking at the graph, I see that there are some people who use all the terms that are listed. Also what I see is that the terms that are the most used are the terms that I see to be least offensive but I can't say anything because I am not a part of any of the mentioned groups. 
     The thing that really got me thinking is that what else would people call these other people?  Seeing that 13% of people wouldn't say the term "Hispanic" kind of surprised me. It really got me thinking on the other names for the people mentioned. I thought really hard for about 2 minutes and couldn't think of anything. So I was and still am really curious to see what others call this group of people.
     Lastly, I thought who in my life calls this group this term or that term. Everyone I have heard reference the first group, I have heard them call them Hispanic and for the second group Asians, for the third, African American, and fourth, person of color. It got me thinking why. Do people use the term they think least offensive or do people use the word they were thought to use. If I were to make the graph, I would call it, "What would you say?".

raw_comment:
As I was reading the graph I couldn’t help but see an ongoing pattern . The terms that are often mentioned in the media are the terms that are winning by a landslide. The terms that are not commonly used in the media are all under 35%. The data tells me that the participants had 2-3 words they could choose from. A lot of the terms are very vague and widely used to talk about a big group of people so yeah that term would win, even if the other terms are better to describe, they are just not widely known enough. 
 		A percentage that stood out to me is that  87% out of 4,423 people said that they use the term Hispanic. The next closest answer is Latina with 70%. This data told me that most people are comfortable enough to use both of those terms
       I think a way to get a better and more honest result is to change the survey from “would you say this word” to what word would you use. Then you can get a most honest reply and the participants can make their own answer for the question. 
	In my community I see all different types of races. My school compared others in my county would be considered one of the least diverse. I would name the graph “We terms do you use?”

raw_comment:
The percentages that stood out to me the most were "person of color" and "nonwhite". I noticed that even though the percentage wasn't over 50% it was still pretty high. I don't agree with using those terms for one it doesn't even make sense, 2 people can be the same color but completely different ethnicity's. Saying nonwhite just makes it seem like any other race besides white is inferiors and is all classified as one. 
I think most of the terms that were used for the chart are pretty common and I think adding more terms and asking more people would help get a more accurate representation on what terms people actually use. Or maybe not even listing terms at all and just asking without giving options would get more of an honest opinion. 
I have never heard anyone use the terms BIPOC, A.A.P.I., or Latinx before so the fact that the percentages were all over 20% with the amount of people that were asked surprised me. I wonder where the people that use those terms grew up and how they were taught about those three terms. 
The people in my community from what I hear use the most common terms the like African American, black, and Asian although I do hear a lot of people use the term Mexican instead of Hispanic which I don't agree with because if you are Mexican that means you're from Mexico and you can still be Hispanic just from different country's so I think Hispanic would be more appropriate for the overall use.

raw_comment:
In this graph, what I noticed the most was how much more the broad terms are used than the more specific terms. Honestly, I don’t use the more specific terms either because I never hear them being said. In the graph, the ones I have heard are the ones that the 4,423 American adults have voted “yes” to using. 
 
  I wonder if the group that was surveyed was all one race or if they were all a mix. Have the words that are not used as much been used way more in the past? I wonder if the more general words are used less in other parts of the world and the specific words are used more. 
 
  I can relate this graph to my life because I hear these words being used everyday, whether it is just in public or at school. Because I never hear the terms most people don’t say, I assume some people may think they are offensive, therefore, they aren’t used as often around others. 
   
The graph is created from a survey of American adults that were asked if they used different terms or not. If I were to make a catchy headline for it, I would name it, “Used or Not Used, What’s the Difference?”

raw_comment:
I notice that the words Americans would say seem to be the ones that are mentioned often in the media. I also noticed that most Americans said they would use the terms Hispanic, Asian, and African American the most and would say Latinx, A.A.P.I, and BIPOC the least.

I wonder if people are not using terms like Latinx, A.A.P.I, and BIPOC because they are afraid of offending others or because they do not understand what those terms mean. I also wonder if they are used less because they are not mentioned in the media as often.

This relates to me and my community because it is important to educate ourselves in terms of different races and ethnicities. With more information, we will be more likely to understand one another and it can lead to less hatred among different groups.

Headline: Educated Speech

I noticed that people are more likely to use words they are used to hearing because that's what's traditional.Its easier to call someone by the traditional term to be respectful.I also noticed that people don't really like to used very specific terms such as "latinix" "A.A.P.I" "BIPOC"

what I wonder 
I wonder if people will don't use terms such as "latinix" "A.A.P.I" "BIPOC" because they may think its offensive to others or just because it feels weird to classify someone by these complicated terms.I also wonder if the people who fall under these more extreme words("latinix" "A.A.P.I" "BIPOC") would consider these offensive or would they believe that there isn't anything wrong with these terms.

how this relates to me 
This relates to me and my community because we live in a society where any little thing can be found as offensive so we need to be more aware of what we say.

raw_comment:
There were many, many great headlines for this graph.  Our appreciation for all that were submitted. Here are only a few:

“As Language Evolves, Americans Weigh In on Words to Describe Race and Ethnicity” by Lainie of Kentucky; “Woke or Broke?: Will Politically Correct Lingo Catch On?” by Clara of Georgetown Visitation Preparatory School; "Words Americans Use When Talking about Identity" by Metropolitan Montessori Middle School in New York City; “Call Me by My Name” by Ashley of Florida; two from Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey – “A New Generation of Terms: Which Do You Identify With?” by Ashley and “Censorship or Respect: Is Terminology Affecting the Way We See Each Other?” by Samuel, and two from Eaglecrest High School in Aurora, Colorado – “What Will America Call Me Today?” by Temsalet and “America Speaks: Words Americans Would and Wouldn't Say” by Ciaran.

There is no graph for next week.  The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 17 with moderation on Wednesday, March 29.  The topic – the Anthropocene.  
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who uses words like most Baby Boomers (habits die hard), and Sara Stoudt, assistant professor of math at Bucknell in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, who as a statistician knows that word choice really does matter.

What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?
I noticed how the biggest percentage of no had been Latinx with 78% of people saying no and in second place had been A.A.P.I. with 73% of people saying no. The terms that people are most comfortable saying Hispanic, Asian, and African American which would most likely be the most common terms used nowadays just based on my personal experience. I noticed this had been taken on dec 1 to dec 4 from Morning Consult. I noticed that they had included additional words in the survey such as "master bedroom'" and "birthing parent".
What do you wonder?
I wonder if the people who had taken the survey were members of the company they said no to. Or if it had just been randomized so these terms may not even apply to the people answering the survey. I wonder how having additional words in the survey could have affected the results. Along with why do people feel more comfortable using traditional terms.
How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I since I am hispanic and have been able to see first hand how some people feel about the latinx term. Understanding it is supposed to be a gender neutral term but some people feel rather that it is invalidating and don't like the word overall.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that people seem to not want to say words that they most likely don't understand like Latinx, AAPI, or BIPOC. That could be a reason why those words have more than 70% of "No"s than "Yes". On the contrary, the most agreed on word would be "Hispanic" with 87% saying yes. I also notice that "Person of color" is the only one that has 50/50 in its results.

2. I wonder what makes someone not want to say any of the words mentioned? Could it be the way they think society will view them or jus their personal thoughts/opinions? I also wonder, why some people don't want to use terms like AAPI and BIPOC? Could it be because it seems weird to refer to someone as an acronym?

3. This relates to me and my community because in the latino community, not everyone has gotten used to the word "Latinx" since it is somewhat new. Seeing this graph lets me see that many others aren't accepting of that term. But, since I live in a diverse community, this graph allows me to see a piece of what people would see as an approrpriate term to call someone without offending. 

4. "Watching What You Say: Could Certain Terms be Offensive?"

raw_comment:
What do you notice
I notice that out of all of the terms used, Latinx is used the least with 22% of the people asked saying they use the term. In contrast, the most agreed upon term is Hispanic with 87% of the people asked saying they use it. It seems that most of the Americans that were questioned stick to more of the older sayings such as Hispanic, Asian/Asian American, and Black/African American and are much less familiar and/or uncomfortable with using the other terms, given the percentages of each of the terms.


What do you wonder?
I wonder why Latino/Latina is used by less of the people asked than Hispanic is considering they’re almost the same and the only difference is the assigning of the masculine and feminine in the words. I’ve also never heard of A.A.P.I. or BIPOC and after doing some research I found that they mean “Asian American/Pacific Islander” and “Black Indigenous Person of Color” respectively. I wonder if the Americans said they didn’t use those terms because they haven’t heard of it like me, or if it’s due to something else.


How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because there are people that come from many different backgrounds in my town and more specifically in my school. And seeing what other people are okay and not okay with saying can be insightful to avoid referring to someone as something they may find offensive.

Headline
Breaking News: Study Reveals Words Americans Refuse to Say

raw_comment:
1. I notice that "BIPOC" "A.A.I.P" and "Latinx are the terms least used by Americans,  and they are  most comfortable using terms such as "Latino" "Asian" and "African-American". I also notice that people didn't feel comfortable saying terms that and fairly new.

raw_comment:
I notice that people use terms that have been around longer. They are more apprehensive about using newer, more inclusive terms. Terms related to nonwhiteness, they have very low usage rates.
I wonder why people are so apprehensive to use these terms, and why terms like "black, and Hispanic are so high up in usage". I wonder why "African-American" is such a highly used inclusive term, while all other inclusive terms are used at such a low rate.  
Many of these terms describe people in my community, and many in my community choose to reject or embrace these words. In my community of most Hispanic people, our terms of self-expression are different from how many people outside of our community refer to us. 
Linguistic evolution: how our terms change over time

1) What I notice is a poll being held on where many were surveyed and on what words Americans would and would not say. The green part of the line stands for what they would say and the pink stands for what they wouldn't say. The names mentioned in this poll include, hispanic, latino/latina, latinx, asian, asian american, aapi, african american, black, person of color, nonwhite, and bipoc. 3) This relates to me and my community because today's generation is constantly learning about new names relating to races and also, my community's population is 90 percent hispanics/latinos(as). 

4) What Would You Call Us?

raw_comment: “Word of the Residents”. That's what I feel the graph should be named . The graph stands out to me for various reasons but the biggest one is the significant difference in the amount of people who would rather use very broad terms when describing races, rather than being specific. 87% of people feel comfortable saying “Hispanic” but only 22% of people would use the word “Latinx”. I’m not sure if there's a deeper reason to why people use the less specific terms, or if  they don’t want to mislabel someone. I also am not sure how true the results could be or if the participants of the survey just said what they felt would look good to the public eye, or followed trends of other people. I say this because individuals around me everyday can be very obvious when talking about others, especially people who aren't the same race as them.

What do you notice?
In this graph we are shown different terms that Americans are most likely to use when referring to a group. I noticed that people are most likely to say a specific race then a term like "POC", "BIPOC" or "Nonwhite". In the first group americans are most likely to use the term Hispanic, in the second group they are most likely to use the term Asian, in the third group they are most likely to use African American. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder what is affecting Americans to use the other terms, does it cancel culture? I wonder if the way these Americans grew up affects the term they use. I also wonder who they surveyed, what age they were, what part of the world they lived in etc. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because I am apart of a generation that really cares about what terms are used to refer to people, I live in a hispanic community and the term that is mainly used here to describe us would be "hispanic".

raw_comment:
The graph displays words that Americans would or would not say. The green represents words that they would not say, while the pink represents words that they would say. I noticed that the words that people are most likely to say are, "Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Black."

I wonder what causes certain words to gain popularity. I also wonder the age demographic of the people polled.

I observed that the words that people were most willing to say were the ones that have been in circulation the longest. The words that the most people said they would not use were, "Latinx, AAPI, and BIPOC", which have all been used recently. Therefore, the longest the words are in use the more likely people are willing to say them.

This relates to me because I have been hearing the emergence of all of these words recently in my community. I am watching as some of these newer words gain prominence and notability. 

Headline: "The Identifiers of America"

raw_comment:
1)Due to tradition, people are more prone to employ terms that they are familiar with and at ease with. In lieu of being accurate and respectful, it is simpler to refer to someone by their conventional name. I believe that the older terminology is still in use since it is clearer and simpler. Although insulting, the terms "Asian", "Black", and "Hispanic" are far simpler to remember and pronounce than "A.A.P.I", "latinX", and "BIPOC".
2)I'm curious how long it will take for the more recent, precise terminology to become commonplace. If they are used frequently enough, they will eventually overtake the current descriptive phrases and cease to exist. I'm curious as to why "Black American" is the only politically correct phrase that has more usage than its opposite.
3). I would argue that this refers to my community as well as this generation in general since it is getting more objectionable to use terms that were not offensive ten years ago. There is a significant contrast between the terms that some people would say that would be thought to be non-offensive and the language that many people would use that would today be considered to be offensive, especially living in a more progressive area but remaining in the south.
4)Be careful what you say—what will be considered suitable or offensive?

raw_comment:
People are more likely to use the words they are used to and comfortable with because that's what's traditional. It is easier to call someone the traditional term at the cost of being correct and respectful. I think people use the old terms because they are simpler and easier to remember.  “Asian”, “black”, and “hispanic”, while disrespectful, are a lot easier to remember and say than “A.A.P.I” , “latinX”, and “BIPOC”.
I wonder how long it will take for the newer, more specific terms to be used. Eventually if they are used enough they will become what is traditional and the descriptive terms we use now won't be around and commonly used.
It really doesn't relate to me or my community personally but it's still important to use the correct terms when referencing people or talking to them because communities overlap, and you talk to plenty of people outside of your community. If someone has a more appropriate term for their ethnicity and lineage you should use it to respect their heritage

Especially living in a more progressive part yet still in the south there is a large difference between words certain people would say that would be considered as non offensive versus many people that would use words that are now deemed as offensive
4. “Overkill vs Offensive”

raw_comment: I notice that the graph shows there is a majority of Americans that prefer to use general, basic terms to describe people of different ethnicity groups. For example, 87% of people would say to use the term “Hispanic” while only 22% would use “Latinx.” I wonder if the race and gender of those surveyed affects the words people would and wouldn’t say? I also notice that in the first three categories there is more comfortability in saying certain words for most Americans. For example, 81% would say “Asian.” However, the last category had more “no” than “yes.” 51% say they would not use the term “person of color.” 62% say they would not use the term “nonwhite.” 70% would not use the term “BIPOC.” I wonder why they are not comfortable using the term person of color, but more comfortable using specific terms to describe ethnicities and races? How do people of different races and ethnicities prefer to be labeled as? This affects me because I am definitely cautious and conscientious of not offending people by calling them an offensive term or one that I am unfamiliar with. My headline is “To Say or Not to Say: Terms Americas Would and Would Not Say”

They do this because most people do not want to offend people, whether it be on purpose or obliviously. I wonder how people who are part of the groups described feel about the use of these words.

raw_comment:
I notice that in this graph, it shows different terms that Americans use or inclined to use when referring to a minority group. Some of the terms that were listed in thie graph are African American, Black, Asia, Asian American, Hispanic, Latino/Latina, A.A.P.I, and more. In the section of the first term, Americans favor to use Hispanic than Latino/a or Latinx that has a 22% in favor. The most common word an American would describe a minority is Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Person of Color and the least word to describe would be Latinx, A.A.P.I, Black, BIPOC.

I wonder if their race/ethnicity has a major factor in this graph and how that affects this graph, to look more deeper into how people choose to say based on their ethnicity/race. It is possible that factors were considered to make this chart or it was just randomly?

This relates to me and my community because even I understand and comprehend why some words are used more than other while describing ethnicity race. I am Latina and  I understand why the word Latinx is not used frequently since its a term that has been used not that long ago to not describe genders, although that is understandable, it is not necessary as the word Hispanic and Latino/a have been doing just fine for decades and used to described anyone with the heritage of Latin. 

Racial and Culture: How does the average American in a Morning Consult describes you?

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
From looking at this graph, I notice that the third word in each row, such as “Latinx,” “A.A.P.I,” “Black,” and “BIPOC” were used the least in their category. For example, the first row of data collected responses on whether Americans would use “Hispanic,” “Latino/Latina,” and “Latinx.” And, out of those three words, Americans said they would not say “Latinx.”
 
What do you wonder?
From looking at this graph, I wonder who was surveyed? What effect would the age and ethnicity of an individual being questioned have on their response?


What’s going on in this graph?
In this graph, 4,423 Americans were surveyed on words they would and wouldn’t say relating to the ethnicity of an individual.


How does this relate to you and your community?
This graph relates to me and my community because I am part of a generation that prioritizes using the correct terminology and I myself feel it is important to use the correct terminology, to make all people feel safe and included.

raw_comment:
What do I notice? 
- Americans are least likely to say "Latinx" and most likely to say "Hispanic" out of every word and phrase listed. 
- There seems to be a lot more debate over the last section ("Person of color", etc.), as the percentages tend to be a lot closer than others. 
- The terms "African American" and "Black" are very close percentage wise (77% yes & 75% yes).
What do I wonder? 
- For some of these terms, does maybe not knowing their meaning play into people being less likely to say them? 
- How would the location(s) this survey was taken in affect the results? 
- Would these results differ if the survey was taken in a different country? 
- How would the unweighted results look compared to the ones shown on this graph? 

What do I think is going on in this graph? 
- This graph shows 11 terms related to various races/ ethnicities, and shows how likely Americans would or would not be to use these terms (the results are weighted to represent Americans as a whole). 
How does this relate to you and your community? 
- This relates to my community and me since, I know in my life people tend to be uncomfortable or hesitant to say some of the words listed. A lot of the times, the reason comes down to either not understanding what the term actually means, or thinking that it may generalize or be inaccurate. 
Title: 
- Will They or Won't They? How Likely Americans are to say Certain Words

1.I noticed that the word the least Americans feel comfortable using is Latinx. I also noticed that the terms I don't really recognize are also the terms Americans wouldn't say like A.A.P.I. and BIPOC. I noticed that the terms that have been around for longer are more frequently used.

I agree with most of the people not using the term Latinx because as a Latina, it is something I would not say myself. I think the term was created to fit our generation but it contradicts the roots of our language.

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs are about what proportion of Americans use specific words to describe some ethnicities and races.  The results come from an online survey of 4,423 adults in December 2022. The survey was weighted on gender, age, race, education and region, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1 percentage point. Word choice is extremely contextual, so they asked people simply if they used a term, not whether they preferred one term over another.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs.  
You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 17 with moderation on Wednesday, March 29.  The topic – the Anthropocene!

- Does **not** use faceting or small multiples.

|---|---|---|

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC are the labels most rarely used by Americans. Hispanic, Asian, African American and Person of Color are the most often used words. The least used and most recent comment on the list is Latinx, which refers to all Hispanics. The words with the lowest popularity on the graph are more contemporary expressions that have gained popularity due to racial strife and the expansion of social media. 

What do you wonder?
In what ways are terms like Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC more inclusive for groups who feel they should be referred to in this way? I'm curious where other terminologies like these comes from. Is there a rise in the use of gender-neutral language as society moves closer to a more accepting culture of all genders, nationalities, and other characteristics?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This applies to my community because there are numerous races represented in my high school, but I was unaware that only a few phrases were used to describe them. For instance, I hear the terms "Hispanic" and "Mexican" much more frequently than terms like "Latino" or a description of the sort of Latino. In contrast, I only hear the word "Black" at our school, where there are hundreds of different students of African heritage. It appears that only generic terminology and a very small number of other words or races are recognized. 

What is going on in the graph?
Which of the Modern Generation's Phrases Do You Connect With?

raw_comment:
1) I notice around 80% of people are comfortable with the use of the terms “Hispanics”, “Asian”, and “African American” while less than 50 percent use the terms “person of color”, “nonwhite”, and “BIPOC”, evident in the contrast of green and pink graphs, showing the dissimilarity of the term's use. I notice acronyms such as BIPOC and A.A.P.I. are severely underutilized with 30% and less, present in the graph.

2) Is the 4,423 Americans an accurate representation of the U.S. population as a whole and how the results of the graph would change if possibly more factors or variables were introduced? What was the racial composition of those who responded to the survey and what was the count of each race? What makes some terms more objectionable than others? What would ethnicities prefer in regard to the chart's terms? Why are the more inclusive terms used least commonly?

3) This relates to me and my community because as a Hispanic, the term Latinx feels redundant, replacing conventional Spanish grammar that would normally utilize "o" and "a" to distinguish between genders with an "x". Terms such as A.A.P.I and BIPOC are acronyms so I would understand why they are least commonly used, but it is interesting that society seems to stray from the more inclusive terms in preference for terms more simple and narrow.

4) American Perception of Racial Identity in Simplest Terms

4. What do they call you? What would you say?
We are all different?

raw_comment:
1) I notice that the graph consists of terms that are used in different minorities and the popularity among these terms. The terms that were listed in the graph are Hispanic, Latino/Latina, Latinx, Asian, Asian American, A.AP.I, African American, Black, Person of color, Nonwhite, BIPOC. I notice that for the first three terms, Americans prefer to use the term “Hispanic” over other terms such as latinx where hispanics have a 87% rate of being used over latinx which only has a 22% rate of being used. Latino/Latina comes second in preferred terms with 70% of people saying they would use the term.
2) I'm curious where other terminology like latinx, A.A.P.I, and BIPOC came from, and how they are more inclusive for groups that believe they should be referred to in this manner. Is there an increase in the number of people who use gender neutral phrases as society develops toward a more welcoming culture of all genders, ethnicities, and so on? 
3) This is relevant to me and my community since I am a Salvadoran woman, thus I am hispanic and Latina because my family and I are from a Central American nation. I also reside in a town full of individuals from Latin America who identify as Hispanic or Latino, which is fascinating to compare to the chart because I have never heard any of my peers use the word Latinx. 
4)  A New Generation of Terms: Which Do You Identify With?

raw_comment:
Americans: Race Words, Are they "Okay" to Say
I notice that 87% of Americans would say the word "Hispanic" whereas only 22% would say "Latinx". It appears that within races, there is always a word people prefer to say over others. This can also be seen in the Asian race with "Asian" at 81% and "A.A.P.I" at 27%. I wonder why people aren't more inclusive on phrases and words as they begin to become more prevalent in our lives. The words "Person of color" and "BIPOC" are brought up more and more throughout our daily lives, yet less than 50% would use those words. I don't understand why because they aren't harmful words, etc. This relates to my community because in my high school we have hundreds of different races, but I never noticed there were only select words used. For example, I hear "Hispanic" or "Mexican" a lot more than other words like "Latino" or specifying the type of latino. On the other hand, there are hundred of different kids of African descent at our school, and all I hear is "Black". It seems like there are just very few recognition of other words or races and only generalized terms. This graph shows the percent of Americans who say or don't say specific "race words".

raw_comment:
1. Americans are least likely to use the terms Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC. The most common words are Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Person of Color. Latinx, which is intended to include all Latinos, is the least frequently used and newest word in the list. The least popular words on the graph are more recent expressions that have gained attention due to racial unrest and the growth of social media. This could explain why other terms are more commonly used than these ones, particularly the way America defines races and ethnicities.

2. Why aren't the most inclusive words used more frequently? Is this because the terms are still so new and the majority of people still don't understand them? A.A.P.I. is also much less common than the more straightforward term Asian, whereas both black terms for black people are much closer to what Americans would say when compared to any other race. Maybe because there are as many black Americans as there are white Americans.

3. In relation to my community, I can also understand why some of the terms selected are used more frequently than others. Being Latina, I could also comprehend why the term "Latinx" isn't used more often. This is because it is the most recent and, in my opinion, is not as necessary as people think since the term "Latino," despite being a masculine word, can be used broadly to describe anyone of Latin ancestry.

4. "POC or BIPOC? Preferred Racial Terms by Americans"

raw_comment:
1) What do we notice?

A lot of students noticed that at least one term on the graph was unfamiliar to them, such as "Latinx" and "Nonwhite". According to this chart, black is not an offensive term; this brought up, among students, how to respectfully address someone. Many students felt that some of the words on the chart are difficult to use and still sound respectful. We also noticed that there was nothing on the chart to imply "it depends." Students pointed out that answers could vary depending on the person. Using these words feels very personal to the individual. A lot of people use broader terms like "Asian" and "Hispanic". There are no options for people with mixed races, which we would have liked to see. 

2) What do you wonder? 

Some of my students were confused about some terms, such as AAPI and BIPOC.

3) How does this relate to you and your community.

It helps us to see/discuss what is appropriate when referring to other people.

4) Catchy headlines?

Correct Terminology or Offensive Words?

raw_comment:
I notice a inverse relationship between the percentage of Americans who would say the terms and the percentage of people from the group the term is intended to describe who prefer to be called by that term. 

For example 87% of Americans would say "Hispanic" and only 22% would say "Latinx." It is my understanding that this group of people prefer the more inclusive term "Latinx."

I wonder if age or region of the country are associated with the words the people would and wouldn't say. 

My husband is Filipino. He has been picked on throughout his life. Kids on the school bus would call him "squint eyes." He also felt pressure to perform well in school because he was represented the "model minority." I think there has been an uptick in hate crimes against A.A.P.I. people since COVID. 

I think folx prefer the term "BIPOC." The term includes more people. Therefore, more people feel represented. More people = more power. 

The title I would use is "Label jars, not people."

What I notice:
- the highest percentage of people say “Hispanic” and “Asian” which makes sense because most hospitals use it to learn more about your health background and it’s a general word that I don’t think many people take offense to
- The lowest percentage of people say “Latnix” and “AAPI” which makes sense because it zeroes in on a certain race and many people would probably take offense to a stranger specifying their race
- most of the general race descriptions have a majority of “yes” and the race specific descriptions have a majority of “no”
- person of color is the only one that has a pretty much balanced number of people, which means some say it and some don’t

What I wonder:
* Does “latino” and “latinx” mean the same thing? 
* Why are most people okay with saying “latino” and “hispanic” but not “latinx”? (same thing with asian, asian americans, and “AAPI”)
* why do most people think they would take offense to “BIPOC” and “AAPI” but not “Black” or “Hispanic”?

A headline could be: Offending Race Cloud; What’s Right and What’s Wrong?

What I wonder: What did the racial and ethnic demography of survey-takers look like? 

How this relates to me & my community: My generation, Gen Z, is the most diverse generation in the history of America thus far, and as a society, our language is evolving to reflect that. This graph represents the growing pains of inclusive language in an ever-broadening world.

- **Horizontal 100% stacked bar chart**

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **stacking**: each horizontal bar is split into **Yes** and **No** segments that sum to 100%.
- Uses **grouped spacing** to separate sets of related terms.
- Does **not** use faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Word/term | Categorical/nominal | Row position; text label at left |
| Response category (Yes / No) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (green for Yes, pink for No); stacked bar segment |
| Percentage of respondents | Quantitative | Bar length/width along horizontal position; numeric labels inside segments |
| Related term groupings | Categorical/nominal | Vertical grouping/spacing between rows |
